body:
1. Why Plants Need Protective Tissues

Plants remain exposed to sunlight, wind, changing moisture conditions and physical injury. Their outer tissues protect the internal living cells while permitting necessary exchanges with the environment.

Important protective tissues include the epidermis of young plant parts and the cork that develops as part of the protective covering of many older stems and roots.

2. Epidermis

The epidermis forms the outer covering of young roots, stems and leaves. It is commonly a single layer of closely packed cells, although thicker arrangements occur in some plants.

Epidermal tissue protects the plant against mechanical damage and excessive water loss. On many aerial surfaces, epidermal cells produce a waxy protective covering called the cuticle.

The cuticle reduces evaporation and is especially important where plants experience dry conditions.

Stomata and Guard Cells

Stomata are small openings in the epidermis of leaves and certain other plant parts. Each typical stoma is associated with 2 specialised guard cells that regulate the opening.

Stomata permit gas exchange. Carbon dioxide can enter the leaf for photosynthesis, while oxygen and water vapour may leave through these openings.

The loss of water vapour from aerial plant parts is called transpiration. The opening and closing of stomata influence both gas exchange and water loss.

Root Hairs

Many epidermal cells in the root-hair region form long, slender extensions called root hairs. These increase the surface area available for absorbing water and dissolved minerals from the soil.

3. Cork

As many woody stems and roots grow older, a protective covering develops that includes cork cells. Mature cork cells are generally dead and closely packed.

Their walls contain suberin, a waxy substance that restricts movement of water and gases. Cork therefore helps protect underlying tissues and reduce water loss.

The dead cork cells observed by Robert Hooke in 1665 belonged to this kind of protective tissue.

4. Complex Permanent Tissues

A complex permanent tissue contains more than 1 type of cell working together for a common function. The principal conducting tissues of vascular plants are xylem and phloem.

Both contain specialised cells, but the substances they transport and the organisation of their cells differ.

5. Xylem: Transport of Water and Minerals

Xylem carries water and dissolved mineral substances from the roots towards the aerial parts of a plant. It also helps provide mechanical support.

Xylem contains 4 main cellular components:

  • Tracheids: Elongated conducting cells with thickened walls; they are dead at maturity.
  • Vessels: Conducting structures made of vessel elements that form continuous pathways for water transport; mature conducting elements are dead.
  • Xylem parenchyma: Living cells associated with storage and other supporting activities.
  • Xylem fibres: Mainly provide mechanical strength and are generally dead at maturity.

The main water-conducting components of xylem can function after losing their living contents because their strengthened walls form pathways through which water can pass.

6. Phloem: Transport of Food

Phloem transports dissolved food substances, particularly sugars produced by photosynthesis, from regions of supply to regions where they are needed or stored.

For example, food produced in leaves may be transported to growing shoots, roots, fruits and storage organs.

Important phloem components include:

  • Sieve tubes: Living conducting elements arranged end to end, with perforated sieve plates that permit transport.
  • Companion cells: Living cells associated with the functioning of sieve-tube elements.
  • Phloem parenchyma: Living cells that can store substances.
  • Phloem fibres: Strengthening elements that are generally dead at maturity.

Phloem transport is not simply the downward movement of food. Its overall direction depends on the location of the supplying and receiving parts of the plant.

7. Xylem and Phloem Compared

FeatureXylemPhloem
Main transportWater and mineralsFood substances
Usual transport patternMainly roots towards shootsSupply regions to receiving regions
Major conducting cellsTracheids and vessel elementsSieve-tube elements
Condition of conducting cellsDead at maturityLiving at maturity
Living supportive cellsXylem parenchymaCompanion cells and phloem parenchyma

8. Coordination of Plant Tissues

Plant tissues work together. Root hairs absorb water from the soil. Xylem conducts water towards leaves. Leaf cells use water during photosynthesis, and the sugars produced can be carried through phloem to other parts.

Meanwhile, epidermal tissues reduce uncontrolled water loss, and meristematic tissues produce new cells for continued growth.

Prelims focus

  • Epidermis protects plant surfaces; the cuticle reduces water loss.
  • Stomata enable gas exchange and transpiration.
  • Root hairs increase the surface available for absorption.
  • Cork cells are generally dead and contain suberin in their walls.
  • Xylem transports water and minerals; phloem transports food.
  • Trap: Xylem parenchyma is living, while most mature xylem conducting cells are dead.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 6, Section 6.2.2, pp. 71–72; GCERT, Science, Standard 9, Chapter 6, pp. 63–64; NCERT, Exploration, Class 9, Chapter 3, Section 3.2, online text consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Plant Protective Tissues and Vascular Transport: Epidermis, Xylem and Phloem

body:
1. The 4 Main Types of Animal Tissues

Animals contain different tissues specialised for protection, support, movement and communication. At the school level, animal tissues are classified into 4 major groups:

  • Epithelial tissue: Covers surfaces, lines cavities and performs functions such as protection, absorption and secretion.
  • Connective tissue: Supports, binds and connects different parts of the body.
  • Muscular tissue: Contracts to produce movement.
  • Nervous tissue: Receives and transmits signals.

These tissues cooperate in organs. For example, the intestine has epithelial tissue for absorption, connective tissue for support, muscular tissue for movement and nervous tissue for coordination.

2. Epithelial Tissue

Epithelial tissue forms coverings and linings on body surfaces and internal organs, with closely packed cells and very little space between adjacent cells.

Epithelium commonly rests on a supporting basement membrane. Its arrangement allows it to form a continuous protective layer or a controlled surface for exchange and secretion.

The shape and number of cell layers are closely related to the function of the tissue.

Simple Squamous Epithelium

Simple squamous epithelium consists of a single layer of thin, flat cells. It provides a short pathway for movement of substances.

It occurs in the walls of lung alveoli, where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged, and in the lining of blood vessels.

Stratified Squamous Epithelium

Stratified squamous epithelium contains several layers of cells. The multiple layers protect against friction and wear.

It occurs in the outer layer of the skin and in protective linings such as those of the mouth and oesophagus.

The key distinction is the number of layers: a single thin layer favours rapid exchange, while many layers provide better protection against mechanical injury.

Cuboidal Epithelium

Cuboidal epithelium consists of cells that appear approximately cube-shaped. It commonly participates in secretion and absorption while providing a lining.

Examples include the lining of kidney tubules and certain glandular ducts.

Columnar Epithelium

Columnar epithelium contains relatively tall, pillar-shaped cells. It is suited to functions such as absorption and secretion.

It occurs in the intestinal lining, where absorbed nutrients pass across the epithelial barrier.

Ciliated Epithelium

Some epithelial cells possess movable hair-like projections called cilia. In parts of the respiratory tract, coordinated ciliary movement helps move mucus and trapped particles along the airway.

Ciliated epithelium is therefore associated with movement of material along a surface rather than contraction of the whole tissue.

Glandular Epithelium

Glandular epithelium consists of epithelial cells specialised to produce and release substances. Examples include cells involved in secreting mucus, digestive substances or other glandular products.

3. Comparing Epithelial Tissues

TypeStructureTypical locationMain function
Simple squamous1 thin, flat layerLung alveoliRapid exchange
Stratified squamousSeveral layersSkin, mouthProtection
CuboidalCube-shaped cellsKidney tubulesAbsorption and secretion
ColumnarTall cellsIntestinal liningAbsorption and secretion
CiliatedCells bearing ciliaRespiratory tractMovement of mucus
GlandularSecretory cellsGlandsSecretion

4. Connective Tissue

Connective tissue supports, connects, binds or protects other tissues and organs. Its cells are embedded in an extracellular matrix that varies in composition and consistency.

Unlike epithelial tissue, which contains closely packed cells, connective tissue often has considerable material between its cells. This material is called the matrix.

The matrix may be liquid, soft, flexible or hard. Its characteristics help determine the function of each connective tissue.

5. Types of Connective Tissue

Blood

Blood is a fluid connective tissue. Its liquid matrix is called plasma. Red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets are suspended in the plasma.

Blood transports gases, nutrients, hormones and wastes. Its cellular components also contribute to defence and blood clotting.

Bone

Bone is a strong supporting connective tissue. Its cells are embedded in a hard matrix containing mineral substances, particularly calcium and phosphorus compounds.

Bone supports the body, protects organs and provides attachment points for muscles.

Cartilage

Cartilage is a supportive connective tissue with a firm but comparatively flexible matrix. It occurs in structures such as parts of the nose, external ear, trachea and joints.

Cartilage can withstand pressure while allowing more flexibility than bone.

Tendon

A tendon connects muscle to bone. It contains strong fibrous material that helps transmit the pulling force produced by muscular contraction.

Ligament

A ligament connects bone to bone, especially around joints. Ligaments help stabilise joints while permitting an appropriate range of movement.

Areolar Tissue

Areolar connective tissue fills spaces between structures, supports internal organs and contributes to tissue repair. It occurs beneath the skin and around many blood vessels, nerves and organs.

Adipose Tissue

Adipose tissue contains cells specialised to store fat. It is found beneath the skin and around some internal organs.

Its functions include energy storage, cushioning and thermal insulation.

6. Matching Connective Tissue with Function

TissueDefining featureMain function
BloodFluid plasma matrixTransport
BoneHard mineralised matrixSupport and protection
CartilageFirm, flexible matrixFlexible support
TendonStrong fibrous tissueMuscle-to-bone connection
LigamentStrong, relatively elastic tissueBone-to-bone connection
AreolarLoose supporting matrixPacking and repair
AdiposeFat-storing cellsStorage and insulation

Tendon connects muscle to bone. Ligament connects bone to bone. Both are connective tissues, but the structures they join are different.

7. Structure Determines Function

Simple squamous epithelium is thin because rapid movement of gases is important in the lungs. Stratified squamous epithelium is multilayered because mechanical protection is important in the skin.

Similarly, blood has a fluid matrix because it must circulate, while bone has a hard mineralised matrix because it must support the body.

These examples illustrate a central principle of tissue biology: the structure of a tissue is related to the function it performs.

Prelims focus

  • Simple squamous epithelium supports rapid exchange in lung alveoli.
  • Stratified squamous epithelium provides protection in the skin.
  • Columnar epithelium occurs in the intestine; cuboidal epithelium occurs in kidney tubules.
  • Blood is a connective tissue with a fluid matrix called plasma.
  • Bone has a hard mineralised matrix; cartilage provides more flexible support.
  • Trap: Tendons connect muscles to bones, while ligaments connect bones to bones.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 6, Sections 6.3.1–6.3.2, pp. 73–75; GCERT, Science, Standard 9, Chapter 6, pp. 65–67; NCERT, Exploration, Class 9, Chapter 3, Section 3.3, online text consulted 3 November 2026.]
